g.text: Long-term conversational assistants must recall information from extensive
interaction histories spanning weeks or months (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=2) Long-term conversational assistants must recall information from extensive interaction histories spanning weeks or months (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2023).

g.text: As these histories grow beyond context window limits, retrieval-augmented
approaches become essential: given a user query, the system retrieves
relevant past conversation rounds to inform its response (Gao et al., 2023).
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=1) As these histories grow beyond context window limits, retrieval-augmented approaches become essential: given a user query, the system retrieves relevant past conversation rounds to inform its response (Gao et al., 2023).

g.text: The effectiveness of such memory systems depends critically on how
conversation rounds are indexed for retrieval.
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) The effectiveness of such memory systems depends critically on how conversation rounds are indexed for retrieval.

g.text: Current systems index user utterances only
Current conversational memory systems predominantly index only
user utterances, treating each round's user turn as the retrieval
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Current conversational memory systems predominantly index only user utterances, treating each round's user turn as the retrieval key (Maharana et al., 2024).

g.text: Assumes users query own past info
This design reflects an implicit assumption that users query about
g.title: N5 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) This design reflects an implicit assumption that users query about information they previously provided.

g.text: However, the LongMemEval benchmark (Wu et al., 2024) identifies a
questions—where users ask about information the assistant provided
in earlier turns, such as "What restaurant did…
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=1) However, the LongMemEval benchmark (Wu et al., 2024) identifies a distinct category of queries—single-session-assistant (SSA) questions—where users ask about information the assistant provided in earlier turns, such as "What restaurant did you recommend last week?"

g.text: For SSA queries, the relevant information resides in assistant responses,
creating a fundamental mismatch with user-only indexing.
g.title: N7 [Limitation] (cites=0) For SSA queries, the relevant information resides in assistant responses, creating a fundamental mismatch with user-only indexing.

g.text: A natural solution is to concatenate user and assistant text into
g.title: N8 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) A natural solution is to concatenate user and assistant text into a single embedding.

g.text: However, this approach suffers from cross-field interference:
mixing semantically different content in one embedding dilutes
g.title: N9 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, this approach suffers from cross-field interference: mixing semantically different content in one embedding dilutes query-relevant features.

g.text: Our experiments confirm this hypothesis—concatenation improves SSA recall
but causes catastrophic degradation on other query types (−0.145 overall
Recall@10), making it unsuitable for production deployment.
g.title: N10 [Result] (cites=0) Our experiments confirm this hypothesis—concatenation improves SSA recall but causes catastrophic degradation on other query types (−0.145 overall Recall@10), making it unsuitable for production deployment.

g.text: We propose fielded max-sim keying, which treats each conversation round as a
two-field document with separate embeddings for user and assistant content.
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) We propose fielded max-sim keying, which treats each conversation round as a two-field document with separate embeddings for user and assistant content.

g.text: The relevance score is the maximum similarity across fields, providing a
natural field selection mechanism: user-centric queries match the user field
while SSA queries match the assistant field.
g.title: N12 [Method] (cites=0) The relevance score is the maximum similarity across fields, providing a natural field selection mechanism: user-centric queries match the user field while SSA queries match the assistant field.

g.text: This approach requires no additional training—only a change in indexing and
g.title: N13 [Method] (cites=0) This approach requires no additional training—only a change in indexing and scoring.

g.text: We demonstrate a zero-harm property: fielded max-sim achieves
identical overall Recall@10 (0.664) to user-only indexing while
improving SSA Recall@10 by +0.018 and NDCG@10 by +0.038, enabling
risk-free adoption as a drop-in replacement.
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We demonstrate a zero-harm property: fielded max-sim achieves identical overall Recall@10 (0.664) to user-only indexing while improving SSA Recall@10 by +0.018 and NDCG@10 by +0.038, enabling risk-free adoption as a drop-in replacement.

g.text: We provide empirical evidence of cross-field interference in
concatenation-based indexing, which degrades overall Recall@10 by
−0.145 despite improving SSA recall, explaining why naive field
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We provide empirical evidence of cross-field interference in concatenation-based indexing, which degrades overall Recall@10 by −0.145 despite improving SSA recall, explaining why naive field combination fails.

g.text: We compare max-sim against linear mixture scoring and show that
only the non-linear max operator achieves zero-harm—linear
mixtures trade SSA gains for unacceptable overall degradation.
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We compare max-sim against linear mixture scoring and show that only the non-linear max operator achieves zero-harm—linear mixtures trade SSA gains for unacceptable overall degradation.
